[23/11/25, 10:58:44 PM] Dinesh: # Minimal: Synthetic object-detection (MNIST) — two CNN variants (baseline, deeper w/BN+Dropout) + Acc & IoU
import numpy as np, tensorflow as tf, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from tensorflow.keras import layers, models

# (optional) uploaded file path (kept per session)
docx_path = "/mnt/data/6d42a7ec-2847-4f93-a2f4-7681bc8941bc.docx"

# --- synthetic dataset builder ---
def make_canvas_set(x,y,n=8000,img=64,dig=20,seed=42):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); X=np.zeros((n,img,img),dtype='float32')
    cls=np.zeros(n,dtype='int32'); bbox=np.zeros((n,4),dtype='float32')
    for i in range(n):
        idx=rng.integers(0,len(x)); d=tf.image.resize(x[idx][...,None].astype('float32'),(dig,dig)).numpy()[...,0]/255.
        H,W=img,img; h,w=d.shape; top=rng.integers(0,H-h+1); left=rng.integers(0,W-w+1)
        X[i,top:top+h,left:left+w]=d; cls[i]=y[idx]
        cx=(left+w/2)/W; cy=(top+h/2)/H; bw=w/W; bh=h/H; bbox[i]=[cx,cy,bw,bh]
    return X[...,None], cls, bbox

(xtr,ytr),(xte,yte)=tf.keras.datasets.mnist.load_data()
Xtr,ctr,btr = make_canvas_set(xtr,ytr,n=12000)
Xte,cte,bte = make_canvas_set(xte,yte,n=2000,seed=7)
print("Train",Xtr.shape,"Test",Xte.shape)

# --- multitask head ---
def head(x):
    return layers.Dense(10,activation='softmax',name='cls')(x), layers.Dense(4,activation='sigmoid',name='bbox')(x)

# --- models ---
def baseline(inp_shape=(64,64,1)):
    i=layers.Input(inp_shape)
    x=layers.Conv2D(16,3,padding='same',activation='relu')(i); x=layers.MaxPool2D()(x)
    x=layers.Conv2D(32,3,padding='same',activation='relu')(x); x=layers.MaxPool2D()(x)
    x=layers.Conv2D(64,3,padding='same',activation='relu')(x); x=layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    c,b=head(x); return models.Model(i,[c,b],name='baseline')

def deeper(inp_shape=(64,64,1)):
    i=layers.Input(inp_shape)
    x=layers.Conv2D(32,3,padding='same',use_bias=False)(i); x=layers.BatchNormalization()(x); x=layers.Activation('relu')(x)
    x=layers.Conv2D(32,3,padding='same',activation='relu')(x); x=layers.MaxPool2D()(x)
    x=layers.Conv2D(64,3,padding='same',use_bias=False)(x); x=layers.BatchNormalization()(x); x=layers.Activation('relu')(x)
    x=layers.Conv2D(64,3,padding='same',activation='relu')(x); x=layers.MaxPool2D()(x)
    x=layers.Conv2D(128,3,padding='same',activation='relu')(x); x=layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    x=layers.Dropout(0.3)(x); c,b=head(x); return models.Model(i,[c,b],name='deeper')

# --- compile helper ---
def compile_mt(m,lr=1e-3, bbox_w=5.0):
    m.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(lr),
              loss={'cls':'sparse_categorical_crossentropy','bbox':'mse'},
              loss_weights={'cls':1.0,'bbox':bbox_w},
              metrics={'cls':'accuracy'})
    return m

m1=compile_mt(baseline()); m2=compile_mt(deeper())
m1.summary(); m2.summary()

# --- IoU (vectorized) for boxes in [cx,cy,w,h] ---
def iou(b1,b2):
    # to x1,y1,x2,y2
    x1a, y1a, x2a, y2a = b1[:,0]-b1[:,2]/2, b1[:,1]-b1[:,3]/2, b1[:,0]+b1[:,2]/2, b1[:,1]+b1[:,3]/2
    x1b, y1b, x2b, y2b = b2[:,0]-b2[:,2]/2, b2[:,1]-b2[:,3]/2, b2[:,0]+b2[:,2]/2, b2[:,1]+b2[:,3]/2
    xi1, yi1 = np.maximum(x1a,x1b), np.maximum(y1a,y1b)
    xi2, yi2 = np.minimum(x2a,x2b), np.minimum(y2a,y2b)
    inter = np.clip(xi2-xi1,0,1)*np.clip(yi2-yi1,0,1)
    area_a = np.clip(x2a-x1a,0,1)*np.clip(y2a-y1a,0,1)
    area_b = np.clip(x2b-x1b,0,1)*np.clip(y2b-y1b,0,1)
    return inter/(area_a+area_b-inter+1e-9)

# --- train & evaluate (short) ---
EPOCHS=6; BATCH=128
hist={}; results={}
for name,model in [('baseline',m1),('deeper',m2)]:
    h=model.fit(Xtr, {'cls':ctr,'bbox':btr}, validation_split=0.1, epochs=EPOCHS, batch_size=BATCH, verbose=1)
    hist[name]=h
    preds = model.predict(Xte, batch_size=256, verbose=0)
    cls_pred = np.argmax(preds[0],axis=1); bbox_pred = preds[1]
    acc = (cls_pred==cte).mean(); miou = float(iou(bbox_pred,bte).mean())
    results[name]={'acc':round(float(acc),4),'miou':round(miou,4)}
print("Results:",results)

from tensorflow.keras import layers, models
from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.text import Tokenizer
from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.sequence import pad_sequences

pairs=[('hi','hello'),('hello','hi there'),
       ('how are you','i am fine'),
       ('what is your name','i am a chatbot'),
       ('bye','goodbye')]

inp=[q for q,a in pairs]
tgt=["<sos> "+a+" <eos>" for q,a in pairs]

tok_in, tok_out = Tokenizer(), Tokenizer()
tok_in.fit_on_texts(inp); tok_out.fit_on_texts(tgt)

X = pad_sequences(tok_in.texts_to_sequences(inp))
Y = tok_out.texts_to_sequences(tgt)
Y_in  = pad_sequences([y[:-1] for y in Y])
Y_out = pad_sequences([y[1:] for y in Y])

vin, vout = len(tok_in.word_index)+1, len(tok_out.word_index)+1

enc_in = layers.Input((X.shape[1],))
enc_emb = layers.Embedding(vin,64)(enc_in)
_,h,c = layers.LSTM(128,return_state=True)(enc_emb)

dec_in = layers.Input((Y_in.shape[1],))
dec_emb = layers.Embedding(vout,64)(dec_in)
dec_out,_ ,_ = layers.LSTM(128,return_sequences=True,return_state=True)(dec_emb,initial_state=[h,c])
dec_out = layers.Dense(vout,activation="softmax")(dec_out)

model=models.Model([enc_in,dec_in],dec_out)
model.compile("adam","sparse_categorical_crossentropy")
model.fit([X,Y_in],Y_out[...,None],epochs=200,verbose=0)

# --- Inference ---
sos = tok_out.word_index["<sos>"]
eos = tok_out.word_index["<eos>"]
itos = {i:w for w,i in tok_out.word_index.items()}

enc_model=models.Model(enc_in,[h,c])

dh = layers.Input((128,)); dc = layers.Input((128,))
d1 = layers.Input((1,))
d_emb = model.layers[4](d1)
d_lstm = model.layers[5]
d_dense = model.layers[6]
o,hh,cc = d_lstm(d_emb,initial_state=[dh,dc])
o = d_dense(o)
dec_model=models.Model([d1,dh,dc],[o,hh,cc])

def reply(text,steps=10):
    seq = pad_sequences(tok_in.texts_to_sequences([text]),maxlen=X.shape[1])
    h,c = enc_model.predict(seq,verbose=0)
    token = np.array([[sos]]); out=[]
    for _ in range(steps):
        p,h,c = dec_model.predict([token,h,c],verbose=0)
        w = int(np.argmax(p[0,0]))
        if w==eos: break
        out.append(itos.get(w,"?"))
        token=np.array([[w]])
    return " ".join(out)

for t in ["hi","how are you","what is your name","bye"]:
    print("User:",t); print("Bot :",reply(t)); print()

3.1 Functional Requirements
The functional requirements for a system describe what the system should do. These
requirements depend on the type of software being developed, the general approach taken by the
organization when writing requirements. The functional system requirements describe the system
function in detail, its inputs and outputs, exceptions and so on.

3.2 Non-Functional Requirements
Non functional requirements, as the name suggests, are requirements that are not directly
concerned with the specific functions delivered by the system. They may relate to emergent system
properties such as reliability, response time and store occupancy. Alternatively, they may define
constraints on the system such as capabilities of I/O devices and the data representations used in
system interfaces.

4.9 Modules of the Project

4.9.1 Module 1
Module Name:-Create Network
Functionality:-This function will initialize nodes, setup links, define resources for each node
etc... The entire network will be depicted as a graph.
Input:-No. of nodes, node position, node resources, node parameters, link parameters.
Output:-Actual network will be setup with the source and destination nodes identified, this
network will be the input for the module 2.
Algorithm used : name of the algorithm
4.9.2 Module 2
Module Name:- Network Transmission
Functionality:-This function will setup the packet according to the protocol version used and
forward the packet in the network with the help of routers to reach the destination.
Input:-source node, destination node, DNS, IP address, Protocol.
Output: - Log file containing the information delay, no. of packets dropped, throughput,
bandwidth.
4.9.3 Module 3
Module Name:- Analysis of performance
Functionality:-This function will analyze the network and its performance and the result will be
depicted in the form of graphs.
Input:-log file containing the network performance measures.
Output: - Graphs.

[17/12/25, 11:57:23 PM] Dinesh: import java.util.Scanner;

public class CaesarCipher {

    // Common method for both encryption & decryption
    static String caesar(String text, int key) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        key = key % 26;

        for (char ch : text.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isLetter(ch)) {
                char base = Character.isUpperCase(ch) ? 'A' : 'a';
                ch = (char) ((ch - base + key + 26) % 26 + base);
            }
            out.append(ch);
        }
        return out.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter the message: ");
        String msg = sc.nextLine();

        System.out.print("Enter the key: ");
        int key = sc.nextInt();

        String encrypted = caesar(msg, key);
        System.out.println("Encrypted Message: " + encrypted);

        String decrypted = caesar(encrypted, -key);
        System.out.println("Decrypted Message: " + decrypted);

        sc.close();
    }
}

Great question.
**Early engagement velocity** is one of those concepts that separates *real recommendation systems* from toy demos — and it’s very teachable to an intern.

I’ll explain it **conceptually**, then **mathematically**, then **how you should ask the intern to implement it**.

---

## 🧠 What is Early Engagement Velocity (Plain English)

> **How fast a video is getting engagement shortly after it is published**

Not *how much* engagement total — but **how quickly** it starts getting attention.

### Why it matters

* Videos that spike early often **trend**
* Old videos with slow growth shouldn’t dominate
* It’s crucial for **last 24 hrs** ranking

---

## 📊 Core Idea (One Line)

```
Velocity = Engagements / Time since publish
```

But we’ll do it *slightly smarter*.

---

## 🧮 Step-by-Step (Intern-Friendly)

### Step 1️⃣ Define “Early Window”

Pick a window:

* First **1 hour**
* First **3 hours**
* First **6 hours**

For PublicNext videos:
👉 **First 3–6 hours** is realistic.

---

### Step 2️⃣ Weight Different Engagements

Not all actions are equal.

Example weights:

* View = 1
* Like = 2
* Comment = 3
* Share = 5

---

### Step 3️⃣ Compute Early Engagement Score

For each video:

```
early_score =
  (views × 1)
+ (likes × 2)
+ (comments × 3)
+ (shares × 5)
```

Only count events **within early window**.

---

### Step 4️⃣ Compute Velocity

```
velocity = early_score / hours_since_publish
```

Example:

| Video | Early Score | Hours Since Publish | Velocity |
| ----- | ----------- | ------------------- | -------- |
| A     | 120         | 3                   | 40       |
| B     | 200         | 10                  | 20       |

👉 Video A is **more trending**, even with fewer total engagements.

---

## 🧠 Smarter Version (Production-Like)

### Add Time Decay

```
decay_factor = exp(-λ × hours_since_publish)
final_velocity = velocity × decay_factor
```

* λ (lambda): 0.05 – 0.15 (tuneable)
* Penalizes older content automatically

---

## 🧩 Full Trending Score (Putting It All Together)

```
trending_score =
  (α × early_velocity)
+ (β × recent_engagement_24h)
+ (γ × editor_priority)
```

Where:

* α, β, γ are weights
* Editor priority ensures important civic videos don’t disappear

---

## 📦 What You Should Ask the Intern to Implement

### Mandatory

* Calculate early engagement velocity
* Explain why video A > video B
* City-wise ranking
* Last 24 hours window

### Optional (Strong Intern Signal)

* Compare:

  * Without velocity
  * With velocity
* Show ranking changes

---

## 📊 Mock Data Example (You Can Share This)

```json
{
  "video_id": "vid_101",
  "city": "Dharwad",
  "published_at": "2026-02-05T06:00:00",
  "engagements": [
    { "type": "view", "time": "06:10" },
    { "type": "share", "time": "06:40" },
    { "type": "comment", "time": "07:15" }
  ]
}
```

---

## 🚫 Why This Is Not “Just AI”

* No LLM prompt can:

  * Choose windows
  * Tune decay
  * Balance fairness
  * Explain rankings

This is **core recommender engineering**.

---

## 🔥 How You Judge the Intern From This

| If they say…                  | Meaning              |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------- |
| “We need velocity”            | Knows ranking basics |
| “Early spike matters”         | Product intuition    |
| “Decay avoids old domination” | Senior thinking      |
| “Cold start is a problem”     | Excellent            |

---

## 🧠 One Killer Follow-up Question (Ask This)

> “What happens if a video gets fake views in first 30 minutes?”

A strong intern will mention:

* Velocity caps
* Minimum unique users
* Anti-gaming logic

---

* Convert this into **pseudo-code**
* Provide **SQL / Mongo aggregation logic**
* Help design **offline evaluation**
* Extend this to **personalised recommendations**

• Professional Language Only: Never use slang, fillers, or casual phrases such as “Hey”, “Cool”, “Yep”, “Chill”, or “No worries”.

  Example: "Could you elaborate on your specific role in that project?"
• Conversational Flow: Keep your responses relatively concise (usually 1-3 sentences) so the interview feels like a natural two-way conversation, but do not be robotic about it. Avoid long monologues.
• Dynamic Interaction: Do not rigidly stick to a script if the candidate changes the subject slightly. Adapt to their answers. If they already answered a question naturally during the conversation, DO NOT ask it again.
• Intent-First Turn Handling: Before you move to the next interview item, first address the candidate's most recent intent.
  - If they asked you something, answer it briefly.
  - If they gave a vague answer, clarify it.
  - If they gave a real answer, acknowledge that specific answer naturally.
  Only then transition to the next question.
• Conversational Reciprocity: If the candidate asks a light reciprocal question such as "What about you?" or "How are you?", answer it briefly and politely in one short line, then transition back naturally. Do not ignore it.
• Clarification Questions Take Priority: If the candidate asks who you are, which company you represent, which role this is about, or why you are calling, answer that clearly before asking anything else.
  Do not skip past those questions.
• Mixed Reply Handling: If the candidate's turn contains both an answer and a question, answer their question first, then continue from the relevant interview point.
• Skip Casual Small Talk When Needed: If the candidate immediately asks what the call is about, which role this is for, or who you represent right after confirming identity, answer that directly and skip the "How are you doing today?" step.
• Opening Recovery: If the candidate says a short reply like "hello", "yes", or "who is this?" while you are still delivering your initial greeting, do not restart the full greeting word-for-word. ════════════════════════════════════
CORE CONVERSATION RULES
════════════════════════════════════
1. Analyze, then Proceed
   Always analyze the candidate's answer first. If they answered the question fully, move to the next item. If not, ask a follow-up.

2. Talk Less, Listen More
   Your turns should be focused and intentional. If the candidate gives a long answer, acknowledge it appropriately and ask the next question. Do not feel the need to summarize their entire answer back to them.

3. Natural Interruptions
   If the candidate pauses, wait a moment to see if they continue.
   If the candidate interrupts you, you will safely stop talking, so allow them to guide the flow.

4. No Assumptions  
   If any information is unclear or incomplete, politely ask for clarification before proceeding.

5. Professional Reconfirmation  
   Always reconfirm critical information such as compensation and notice period.
   Example: “Just to be precise, you mentioned your current CTC is 10 LPA. Is that correct?”

6. Scheduling Precision
   Never pretend a callback time was confirmed unless the candidate actually provided a usable date and time.
   If they only say "tomorrow", "later", "evening", "after some time", "yeah", or any other vague reply, ask again for the exact time.
   Do not say "I have noted that down" or "I will call you then" unless you truly have both a clear date and a clear time.

7. Do Not Over-Advance
   Do not treat fillers or acknowledgments like "yes", "yeah", "okay", "sure", "tomorrow", or "hmm" as a complete answer to an interview question.
   If the candidate gives a partial, vague, or unclear answer, stay on that topic and ask one short clarifying question.

8. Candidate Questions Must Be Fully Addressed
   If the candidate asks a direct question such as:
   - "What about you?"
   - "Which company are you from?"
   - "Which role is this for?"
   - "Why are you calling?"
   then answer that exact question in a natural way before moving forward.
   Do not partially answer it and then jump to the next scripted item.

════════════════════════════════════
AUDIO & CLARITY HANDLING
════════════════════════════════════
• If a transcript fragment seems garbled or incomplete, use your intelligence to infer what the candidate meant based on the context. 
• If you genuinely cannot understand them after considering context, politely ask them to clarify:
  - "I'm sorry, I didn't quite catch that. Could you repeat?"
• Do not get stuck in a loop of apologizing. If clarify fails twice, gently move the conversation forward.

════════════════════════════════════
CONFIDENCE-AWARE ADAPTATION
════════════════════════════════════
• Continuously assess the candidate’s confidence level (high / medium / low) based on clarity, certainty, and engagement.
• If confidence appears LOW:
  - Simplify the question
  - Shift from theory-based questions to experience-based or high-level questions
• If confidence appears HIGH:
  - Ask one level deeper, but remain calm and non-confrontational
• Never pressure, challenge, or intimidate.

════════════════════════════════════
HANDLING DIFFICULT OR UNCERTAIN RESPONSES
════════════════════════════════════
• If the candidate says "No", "I don't want to answer", "I'm not sure", or "I don't know":
  - Respond warmly and move on:
    "No problem at all. Let's move to the next topic."
    "That's perfectly alright. We can skip this one."
• If the candidate seems disinterested or gives short answers:
  - Keep questions brief and don't push:
    "I understand. Just a couple more quick questions."
• If the candidate says "Not interested" or wants to end:
  - Be gracious:
    "I completely understand. Thank you for your time today. Have a wonderful day."
• NEVER pressure the candidate or make them uncomfortable.
• If they don't know something, simply acknowledge and move on.”


════════════════════════════════════
HANDLING HOLD / WAIT REQUESTS — CRITICAL
════════════════════════════════════
• If the candidate says "hold on", "give me a moment", "just a minute", "wait", "one second",
  "let me check", "can you hold", "2 minutes", or ANY similar request to pause:
  - Respond warmly: "Of course, take your time. I will wait."
  - Then STAY COMPLETELY SILENT. Do NOT speak again until the candidate speaks.
  - Do NOT hang up, end, or terminate the conversation.
  - Do NOT assume they have left. They will come back.
  - If the candidate has not spoken for about 60 seconds after asking you to hold,
    gently check in ONCE: "I am still here whenever you are ready."
  - Then go silent again and continue waiting.
• This is CRITICAL — never cut the call when a candidate asks you to hold.
════════════════════════════════════
════════════════════════════════════
Location Handling Rule — CRITICAL
════════════════════════════════════
• Ask for the candidate’s current base location once and acknowledge it.
• After confirmation, you MAY ask about relocation ONLY in a generalized, future-oriented manner.
• The relocation question must:
  - NOT repeat the candidate’s current location
  - NOT mention specific cities unless the candidate is currently based elsewhere
  - Be framed around potential future project needs
• Approved phrasing examples:
  - “Looking ahead, would you be open to relocation if a future project requires it?”
  - “Some roles may involve location flexibility over time. Would that be acceptable to you?”
• Avoid phrasing that sounds redundant or contradictory.
════════════════════════════════════
INTERNAL EVALUATION — SILENT
════════════════════════════════════
• Maintain an internal, non-verbal evaluation across:
  - Communication clarity
  - Role alignment
  - Technical exposure
  - Professional maturity
• NEVER reveal judgments, scores, or decisions during the conversation.
• Use this internal state only to:
  - Adjust question depth
  - Decide the closing tone

════════════════════════════════════
INTERVIEW FLOW — STRICT SEQUENCE
════════════════════════════════════

1. PROFESSIONAL GREETING  
"Hello, this is {bot_name} from {company_name}'s Talent Acquisition team. Am I speaking with {candidate_name}?"”

→ IF they say "No", "Wrong number", "This is not [name]", or similar:
  - Respond politely: "I apologize for the inconvenience. May I know if [candidate_name] is available at this number, or should I try a different contact?"
  - If they say the person is not available: "No problem. I will try again later. Thank you for your time. Have a good day."
  - If they say wrong number: "I apologize for the confusion. Thank you for letting me know. Have a good day."
  - END the conversation gracefully.”

2. FRIENDLY EXCHANGE (after they confirm identity)
"Great! How are you doing today?"
→ Use this only if the candidate simply confirms identity and does not immediately ask what the call is about.
→ Wait for their response, then acknowledge warmly.
→ If they ask a reciprocal question like "What about you?", answer briefly and politely, for example:
  "I'm doing well, thank you for asking."
→ Then continue the interview naturally.

3. CONTEXT SETTING  
"So, your profile stood out for the {job_title} position, and I would love to have a brief 10-minute screening discussion. Is now a convenient time?"

→ IF, right after identity confirmation, they ask what this call is about, who you are, which company this is, or which role it concerns:
  - Answer directly, for example: "Certainly. This is Monica from {company_name}'s Talent Acquisition team, and this call is regarding the {job_title} position."
  - Then ask whether now is a convenient time.

→ IF they say "No", "I'm busy", "Not now", "Not available", or similar:
  - Ask for callback: "No problem at all. When would be a convenient time for me to call you back? Please share a date and time that works for you."
  - If they provide only a partial answer like "tomorrow" or "evening", ask again for the missing exact time.
  - Only after they provide a clear date and time: "Perfect, thank you for clarifying. I will call you on [repeat their date/time]. Have a pleasant day!"
  - END the conversation gracefully.

→ IF they respond with a clarification question such as asking which company, role, or interview this is about:
  - Answer that first in one or two clear sentences.
  - Then return to whether this is a convenient time.

4. OPENER  
"Excellent. To begin, could you give me a quick overview of your professional background?"”

5. HR ESSENTIALS (Ask one by one, in order)
• "Could you confirm your current base location?"
• "Would you be open to relocation if the role requires it?"
• "May I ask what your current annual compensation, or CTC, is?"
  → ONLY reconfirm if you didn't understand the number clearly
• "What are your salary expectations for your next move?"
  → ONLY reconfirm if you didn't understand the number clearly
• "Is this expectation negotiable, or is it a fixed requirement for you?"
• "Have you already resigned, or are you still serving your notice period?"
• "When would be your last working day?" OR "How long is your official notice period?"”

6. ROLE FIT (Keep it simple and conversational)
"Thank you for sharing. Just a couple of quick questions about your background."
• The configured screening questions for this job are:
{questions_formatted}
• Ask every configured screening question exactly once, one at a time, in the given order.
• Ask them directly and confidently, while still sounding natural and professional.
• Before each configured question, briefly respond to what the candidate just said so the conversation feels human rather than scripted.
• Keep questions simple and non-technical.
• If they don't know or seem unsure, simply say "No worries" and move on.
• DO NOT grill them or ask follow-up technical questions.

{graceful_closing}

[27/04/26, 2:42:11 AM] Diya: NTERNSHIP OBJECTIVES
The key objectives of the internship were:
1. To understand and implement OAuth 2.0 authentication
OAuth 2.0 is a secure authorization framework that allows applications to access user data from external platforms without exposing user credentials. The objective was to understand the complete authentication flow, including user consent, authorization codes, access tokens, and secure API access, and to implement this mechanism in real-world applications.
2. To integrate third-party APIs such as YouTube Data API v3 and Facebook Graph API
Third-party APIs enable applications to communicate with external services and extend their functionality. This objective involved learning how to connect backend systems with APIs like YouTube and Facebook, handle requests and responses, manage permissions, and ensure reliable data exchange between systems.
3. To build scalable backend systems using Node.js and Express.js
Scalable backend systems are designed to handle increasing user requests efficiently without performance degradation. This objective focused on developing server-side applications using Node.js and Express.js, structuring APIs, handling routes, and ensuring that the system can be extended and maintained easily.
4. To implement Redis caching for performance optimization
Caching is a technique used to store frequently accessed data in memory to reduce database load and improve response time. The objective was to implement Redis as a caching layer, configure TTL (Time-To-Live), and understand how cache hits and misses affect system performance.
5. To design a personalization engine based on user behavior
A personalization engine analyzes user interactions and preferences to deliver customized content. This objective involved designing algorithms that consider factors such as user interests, location, trending content, and recency to rank and recommend relevant content dynamically.
6. To improve debugging, testing, and real-world problem-solving skills
Debugging and testing are essential for identifying and resolving issues in applications. This objective focused on developing the ability to analyze errors, test different scenarios, and implement effective solutions to real-world technical challenges encountered during development.
4. TASKS PERFORMED
4.1 Social Media Poster System
A full-stack application was developed to automate posting content on social media platforms.
Key Features:
Upload videos to YouTube with metadata (title, description, tags)
Share links on Facebook pages
Secure authentication using OAuth 2.0
Real-time feedback and error handling
Technical Implementation:
Backend built using Express.js
File uploads handled using Multer
YouTube API used for video uploads
Facebook Graph API used for posting links
Challenges & Solutions:
Fixed OAuth callback errors by implementing proper GET routes
Resolved permission issues by updating API scopes
Managed authentication state effectively in frontend and backend
Outcome:
YouTube integration was fully functional with successful video uploads. Facebook integration was implemented at the backend level but remained partially completed due to account-related restrictions.
4.2 Personalized News Feed System with Redis
A backend system was developed to deliver personalized and high-performance news feeds.
Core Components:
MongoDB for storing user and content data
Redis for caching frequently accessed responses
Personalization engine for ranking content
Key Features:
User-specific content recommendations
Multi-factor scoring (category, district, trending, recency)
Intelligent caching with TTL configuration
Automatic cache invalidation on updates
Performance Results:
Cache Miss: ~43ms
Cache Hit: ~8ms
Achieved approximately 5x performance improvement
Outcome:
The system successfully demonstrated efficient content delivery with reduced database load and faster response times, making it suitable for scalable applications.
5. REFLECTION
This internship provided valuable hands-on experience in backend development and real-world system design.
Key Learnings:
Understanding OAuth 2.0 authentication flow in real applications
Working with external APIs and handling permissions
Importance of caching in improving application performance
Designing scalable and modular backend systems
Challenges Faced:
Debugging OAuth authentication errors
Managing API tokens and permissions
Understanding Redis caching flow and invalidation
Approach to Overcome Challenges:
Step-by-step debugging and testing
Using logs and API testing tools
Breaking down complex flows into simpler steps
This experience significantly improved problem-solving ability and confidence in handling real-world development scenarios.
CONCLUSION
The internship successfully achieved its objectives by developing two major systems: a Social Media Poster and a Personalized News Feed System. These projects provided a comprehensive understanding of modern backend development practices, including API integration, authentication mechanisms, caching strategies, and performance optimization.
The Social Media Poster demonstrated how external platforms like YouTube and Facebook can be integrated into a unified system using secure OAuth 2.0 authentication. The successful implementation of video uploads and automated posting highlighted the importance of handling real-world API constraints, permissions, and error scenarios.
The Personalized News Feed System showcased the effectiveness of Redis caching and personalization algorithms in improving system performance and user experience. By reducing response times from ~43ms to ~8ms, the system proved the practical impact of caching in scalable applications.
Overall, the internship strengthened technical skills in Node.js, Express.js, MongoDB, and Redis, while also enhancing understanding of system design and optimization. It provided valuable exposure to real-world challenges and solutions, preparing for future roles in software development and backend engineering.

[07/05/26, 4:14:15 PM] Dinesh: Q4. Describe the Code of Ethics to be Followed by Hackers
Page Reference: Page 8 (Chapter 1 — Section 1.10)
Now computer security training organizations have an ethical code of conduct that people must agree to abide by in order to be certified by them. The most popular hacker code of ethics on the Internet is the EC-Council Code of Ethics.
The chapter provides a solid, concise code of ethics to operate by, both personally and professionally. "Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution" introduced the world to one of the earliest versions of hacker ethics.

Ethical Hacker Roles and Responsibilities (Page 5 — Section 1.5):
Ethical Hackers must follow certain guidelines in order to perform hacking legally. A good hacker knows his or her responsibility and adheres to all of the ethical guidelines. Here are the most important rules of Ethical Hacking:
•	An ethical hacker must seek authorization from the organization that owns the system. Hackers should obtain complete approval before performing any security assessment on the system or network.
•	Determine the scope of their assessment and make known their plan to the organization.
•	Report any security breaches and vulnerabilities found in the system or network.
•	Keep their discoveries confidential. As their purpose is to secure the system or network, ethical hackers should agree to and respect their non-disclosure agreement.
•	Erase all traces of the hack after checking the system for any vulnerability. It prevents malicious hackers from entering the system through the identified loopholes.
[07/05/26, 4:14:33 PM] Dinesh: Q6. Discuss About the Different Attack Vectors Used by Hackers
Page Reference: Pages 14–16 (Chapter 1 — Section 1.12)
1. Compromised Credentials (Page 14):
Usernames and passwords are still the most common type of access credential and continue to be exposed in data leaks, phishing scams and by malware. When lost, stolen or exposed, credentials give attackers unfettered access. Organizations are now investing in tools to continuously monitor for data exposures and leaked credentials.
2. Weak Credentials (Page 14):
Weak passwords and reused passwords mean one data breach can result in many more. Organizations should teach employees how to create a secure password, invest in a password manager or a single sign-on tool, and educate staff on their benefits.
3. Malicious Insiders (Page 14):
Disgruntled employees can expose private information or provide information about company specific vulnerabilities.
4. Missing or Poor Encryption (Page 14):
Common encryption methods like SSL certificates and DNSSEC can prevent man-in-the-middle attacks and protect the confidentiality of data being transmitted. Missing or poor encryption for data at rest can mean that sensitive data or credentials are exposed in the event of a data breach or data leak.
5. Misconfiguration (Page 14):
Misconfiguration of cloud services, like Google Cloud Platform, Microsoft Azure, or AWS, or using default credentials can lead to data breaches and data leaks.
6. Ransomware (Page 14):
Ransomware is a form of extortion where data is deleted or encrypted unless a ransom is paid, such as WannaCry. Minimize the impact of ransomware attacks by maintaining a defense plan, including keeping your systems patched and backing up important data.
7. Phishing (Pages 14–15):
Phishing is a social engineering technique where the target is contacted by email, telephone or text message by someone who is posing to be a legitimate colleague or institution to trick them into providing sensitive data, credentials or personally identifiable information (PII).
8. Vulnerabilities (Page 15):
New vulnerabilities are added to CVE every day and zero-day vulnerabilities are found just as often. If a developer has not released a patch for a zero-day vulnerability before an attack can exploit it, it can be hard to prevent.
9. Brute Force (Page 15):
Brute force attacks are based on trial and error. Attackers may continuously try to gain access to your organization until one attack works. This could be by attacking weak passwords or encryption, phishing emails or sending infected email attachments containing a type of malware.
10. Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) (Page 15):
DDoS are cyber attacks against networked resources like data centers, servers or websites and can limit the availability of a computer system. The attacker floods the network resource with messages which cause it to slow down or even crash, making it inaccessible to users. Potential mitigations include CDNs and proxies.
11. SQL Injections (Page 15):
SQL stands for structured query language, a programming language used to communicate with databases. An SQL injection uses malicious SQL to get the server to expose information it otherwise wouldn't.
12. Trojans (Page 15):
Trojan horses are malware that misleads users by pretending to be a legitimate program and are often spread via infected email attachments or fake software.
13. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) (Page 15):
XSS attacks involve injecting malicious code into a website but the website itself is not being attacked, rather it aims to impact the website's visitors.
14. Session Hijacking (Pages 15–16):
When you log into a service, it generally provides your computer with a session key or cookie so you don't need to log in again. This cookie can be hijacked by an attacker who uses it to gain access to sensitive information.
15. Man-in-the-Middle Attacks (Page 16):
Public Wi-Fi networks can be exploited to perform man-in-the-middle attacks and intercept traffic that was supposed to go elsewhere, such as when you log into a secure system.
16. Third and Fourth-Party Vendors (Page 16):
The rise in outsourcing means that your vendors pose a huge cybersecurity risk to your customer's data and your proprietary data. Some of the biggest data breaches were caused by third parties

[07/05/26, 10:23:54 PM] Dinesh: Q2. Define Computer Worms with Its Types 
Page Reference: Pages 110–112 (Chapter 6 — Sections 6.1, 6.2) Definition (Page 111): 
Computer worms are replicable in nature hence there is no need of assistance. High Bandwidth is consumed and servers are overloaded with the files that contain the worms and that causes harm to the network. It is also responsible for spreading and destroying the network; the codes written in a program are also destroyed by worm as it is inside systems. The entire network can be destroyed by spam. The codes that are used for program are also called payloads. Computer worms destroy the data stored in the system. Some examples of worms are Morris Worm, Storm Worm, SQL Slammer and so on. 
 
Types of Computer Worms (Section 6.2, Pages 111–112): 
1.	Email Worms (Page 111): 
The email box is worked as a client for worm. It has infected link or it contains some attachment in which the worm is present and after its open the worm gets downloaded into the system. The contacts also are searched by this worm and it sends links so that those systems are also destroyed. A famous example is the ILOVEYOU email worm which infected computers in 2000. 
2.	Internet Worms (Page 112): 
In a technological era, everyone knows about Internet and it is used as a medium to connect with the other machines for vulnerable search and affect them. If the system has not installed antivirus, those systems are affected easily with these worms. 
3.	File-Sharing Network Worms (Page 112): 
In some cases, user downloads the files from some unknown sources like any link or device; such type of files or devices may have the worms which locate a shared folder and destroy other files. A famous example of this type of worm is 'Phatbot' which infected computers in 2004 through sharing files. 
4.	Instant Message and Chat Room Worms (Page 112): 
In this type of worm, the user gets an invitation through some link via email or contact; it acts like human and chat with the other machine via messages. After accepting the invitation and opening the message or link, the system is infected. 
5.	IRC Worms (Page 112): 
The full form of IRC is Internet Relay Chat; this was a messaging application that was created as a unique trend once. These worms are responsible for destroying the contact list of IRC. To destroy this worm, the user needs to scan the system and update the security settings.
[07/05/26, 10:25:19 PM] Dinesh: Q19. Discuss ARP Spoofing with Mechanisms Used for Detection and Prevention 
Page Reference: Pages 99–103 (Chapter 5 — Section 5.10) What is ARP Spoofing? (Page 99): 
When malicious ARP packets are transmitted to a LAN's default gateway, ARP spoofing, also known as ARP poisoning, occurs. This is done to change the ARP table's IP/MAC address pairings. The hacker instructs the gateway that their MAC address should now be linked to the IP address of the target victim. The attacker's IP address is linked to the target's MAC address, and vice versa. The default gateway then caches the updated IP/MAC relationships and distributes them to the rest of the network's devices. 
Steps of an ARP Spoofing Attack (Pages 99–100): 
16.	The attacker gains access to the local network and scans it for IP addresses of devices. 
17.	The attacker forges ARP answers using a spoofing tool like Driftnet or Arpspoof. 
18.	ARP packets with the attacker's MAC and the victim's IP address are sent, tricking the router and PC into connecting to the attacker rather than each other. 
19.	The ARP cache is refreshed, allowing the PC and router to maintain contact with the attacker. 
20.	Other hosts will now transmit data to the attacker instead of the original receiver. 
 
What ARP Spoofing is Used For (Page 100): 
•	DDoS attacks: To initiate a DDoS attack, the attacker might use the address of the server they want to target instead of their own MAC address. 
•	Session hijacking: ARP spoofing can be used to obtain your session ID, which the hacker can then use to gain access to accounts that the victim is logged into. 
•	Continued packet hijacking: The attacker can continue sniffing your packets and taking your information. 
•	Disruption in communication: This would be a man-in-the-middle type of attack. The hacker can intercept and modify traffic, as well as deliver malicious files or websites to the victim's computer. 
 
How to Detect ARP Spoofing (Pages 100–102): 
There are third-party software applications for detecting ARP spoofing. There are two types: 
•	Basic networking tools, such as Wireshark, that allow you to examine all of your network traffic and aid in troubleshooting and analysis. 
•	Applications like XArp, which are designed specifically to detect ARP spoofing and continuously monitor your network. 
Using the OS built-in functionality: Type the command arp -a to see the ARP table. If there are any IP addresses with the same MAC address (referred to as "Physical Address"), this implies that an ARP spoofing attack is taking place. 
 
Prevention of ARP Spoofing (Pages 102–103): 
•	To help identify poisoned ARP packets, use packet filtering. 
•	Avoid trust relationships that need authentication using IP addresses. 
•	Use a Virtual Private Network (VPN): VPNs encrypt all of your communications, rendering your traffic useless to any hacker attempting to spoof your ARP. 
•	Use Static ARP: ARP allows for the creation of static entries for any IP address. 
•	Encrypt data in transit using cryptographic network protocols like TLS, SSH, or HTTPS. 
•	To identify attacks, use ARP spoofing detection software such as Arpwatch and ARP-Guard. 
•	By monitoring address resolution, intrusion-detection software like Snort can assist stop ARP spoofing attempts.
